_meta:
Original curation, not derived from content/grammar_data.py (the scraped-from-jlptsensei.com file -- see THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md and the JLPT mock-exam plan for why). There is no official JLPT grammar list published by JEES/the Japan Foundation; every study site's list is its own independent observation of patterns that recur on real papers, which is why they overlap heavily without copying one another. This file is that same kind of independent curation, cross-checked against multiple such sources during construction rather than lifted from any one of them, holding only the grammar-point identity (pattern name, its attachment structure, a short original gloss, and its conventional level) -- the facts about which patterns exist and roughly where they're taught, not any site's explanations or example sentences. Used by study/exam_grammar_gen.py as the checklist a per-item LLM call generates ORIGINAL example sentences and distractors from; the meaning/structure fields here are deliberately short (a one-line gloss, not an explanation) to stay clearly on the facts side of the line.

205 entries, 41 per level. Level placement follows the modern five-level syllabus (2010-), cross-checked so that each pattern appears at the same level on at least two independently maintained lists. Note that the widely mirrored tanos.co.uk/Wikibooks inventories are the PRE-2010 four-level 出題基準: their '2級' predates N3, which was later carved out of the gap between old 2級 and old 3級, so roughly a third of what they file under 2級 is N3 today. They are useful for confirming that a pattern is examined at all, not for deciding which of N3/N2 it belongs to.

Patterns are deliberately allowed to coincide with grammar_data.py's -- which patterns exist is a fact about the language, not anyone's expression of it. What must never coincide is the wording of structure/meaning, and tests/test_grammar_points.py asserts that verbatim-disjointness on every entry.
